Weighted burden (SUM) multi-trait test

Source: vignettes/method-sum.Rmd
method-sum.Rmd

Function: run_sum()

Result column: sum

Family: Burden-style multiple association

Introduction

MPAT/MTAR multi-phenotype burden test. It collapses the per-trait Z-scores into a single inverse-correlation-weighted linear combination (the optimal GLS contrast for a common cross-trait effect) and tests it with a two-sided normal tail.

Mathematical Framework and Implementation

For a variant with per-trait Z-score vector z=(z1,…,zK)′z = (z_1,\dots,z_K)', zk=β̂k/se(β̂k)z_k = \hat\beta_k / \mathrm{se}(\hat\beta_k), over KK phenotypes, define the weight vector a=Σ−1𝟏a = \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{1}, where Σ\Sigma is the K×KK \times K trait correlation matrix and 𝟏\mathbf{1} is the all-ones vector (aa is precomputed as a in the engine). The burden statistic is the absolute value of the inverse-variance-weighted sum

T=|a′z|=|𝟏′Σ−1z|. T = \left| a' z \right| = \left| \mathbf{1}' \Sigma^{-1} z \right|.

This linear combination is the generalized-least-squares (best linear unbiased) contrast for detecting a common scalar effect shared across all traits.

Under the global null z∼𝒩(0,Σ)z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma) the underlying linear form a′z=𝟏′Σ−1za' z = \mathbf{1}' \Sigma^{-1} z is normal with mean 0 and variance

Var(a′z)=𝟏′Σ−1ΣΣ−1𝟏=𝟏′Σ−1𝟏≡𝚜𝚞𝚖_𝚂𝚒𝚗𝚟, \mathrm{Var}(a' z) = \mathbf{1}' \Sigma^{-1} \Sigma\, \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}' \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{1} \equiv \texttt{sum\_Sinv},

i.e. a′z∼𝒩(0,𝟏′Σ−1𝟏)a' z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, \mathbf{1}'\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{1}). The two-sided p-value is

p=2Pr⁡(𝒩(0,σ)≥T),σ=𝟏′Σ−1𝟏. p = 2\,\Pr\!\left(\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma) \ge T\right),\qquad \sigma = \sqrt{\mathbf{1}' \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{1}}.

What This Method Advances

SUM turns many correlated trait scores into the generalized-least-squares contrast for a common direction of effect.

Assumptions

SUM is a one-degree-of-freedom burden test: it has high power when effects are concordant (shared common direction) across many traits, and is the locally most powerful test for a single common effect after optimally accounting for trait correlation through Σ−1\Sigma^{-1}. It loses power, and can lose it entirely, when effects are heterogeneous in sign so that the weighted contributions cancel, or when signal is sparse and confined to a single trait; the omnibus Wald (run_wald()) or variance-component (run_vc()) tests are preferable there. Validity requires a correctly specified, non-singular Σ\Sigma and approximately Gaussian null Z-scores.

When This Method Is a Good Fit

Good for concordant effects shared across many traits after inverse-correlation weighting.

The implementation treats variants independently and relies on the trait-correlation estimate derived from the available summary statistics unless an individual method estimates a pairwise null moment internally.

Minimal Usage 

library(pleioverse)
set.seed(1)
pleio <- run_pleiosim(
  n_phenotype = 3, n_participant = 500,
  n_variant_pleiotropic = 3,
  n_variant_nonpleiotropic = c(3, 3, 3),
  n_variant_null = 30,
  heritability = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3)
)
pleio <- run_sum(pleio)
head(pleio@results$sum)

Implementation Files

  • R wrapper: R/run_sum.R
  • C++ kernel or dispatcher: src/sum.cpp
  • Shared MPAT inputs, where applicable: R/pleiotest.R and src/test_engine.cpp

References
